title: Vmstat swap-in (si) rate
exclusions: Detects repeated host-level Linux swap-in traffic by deriving a KiB/s rate from adjacent `pswpin` page-counter snapshots. It does not prove memory thrashing, identify the process or cgroup that owns the faulted pages, measure application latency, distinguish demand paging from every workload cause, monitor container memory independently of the host namespace, or replace capacity analysis. It does not treat swap occupancy, `pgpgin`, major faults, the first `vmstat` report, or the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux `pgSwapOut` field as `si`. It makes no security, compliance, prevention, or production-validation claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain the versioned `linux_vmstat_swap_in_rate_5m` saved-search definition and schedule, effective scripted-input and field-extraction configuration, collector checksum, dispatch history, alert rows, source-health results, and dated positive/negative control output. Each finding should preserve `host`, `boot_id`, `window_start`, `window_end`, `observed_buckets`, `breach_buckets`, `average_swapin_kib_s`, `maximum_swapin_kib_s`, `average_swapout_kib_s`, `maximum_major_faults_per_second`, `page_size_bytes`, and the resolved threshold. These artifacts show what the deployed counter feed and search reported; this documentation-only review produced no runtime evidence or operator sign-off.

controlTest.positiveScenario: With the search's `now()` and time bounds fixed, index six one-minute `index=os sourcetype=linux:vmstat_swap source=linux_vmstat_swap` events for `host=si-positive`, `collector_schema=1`, `collector_status=ok`, one `boot_id`, and `page_size_bytes=4096`. Place the samples from 11 through 6 minutes before the fixed dispatch time. Increase `pswpin_pages` by 30,720 pages in each of the first three adjacent intervals and by zero in the last two; keep `pswpout_pages` and `pgmajfault_total` nondecreasing. The five derived buckets must yield one medium-severity result with `observed_buckets=5`, `breach_buckets=3`, each breached rate equal to 2,048 KiB/s, and `maximum_swapin_kib_s=2048`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Repeat the six-event fixture for `host=si-negative`, but make only two of the five adjacent intervals reach 2,048 KiB/s and keep the other three below 1,024 KiB/s; the search must return no result because fewer than three complete buckets breach. Test guards separately: decrease `pswpin_pages`, change `boot_id`, change `page_size_bytes`, create an elapsed gap greater than 150 seconds, omit one candidate minute, and set `collector_status=read_error`. The affected interval or incomplete series must not alert, and no reset, malformed value, or long-gap delta may be converted into a swap-in rate.

dataSources: One key-value event per host per minute in deployment-selected `index=os`, `source=linux_vmstat_swap`, and `sourcetype=linux:vmstat_swap`, emitted by a locally managed Universal Forwarder scripted input. It reads cumulative page counters `pswpin`, `pswpout`, and `pgmajfault` from `/proc/vmstat`, the base page size from `getconf PAGE_SIZE`, the boot identity from `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, and the sample epoch from the host clock. The custom contract is required because native `vmstat(8)` displays `si` as a rate, while the standard Splunk Add-on `vmstat` source type does not document a native `si` field contract.
app: Locally managed deployment app `TA-linux-vmstat-swap` containing the read-only collector, scripted input, search-time key-value extraction, saved search, and dashboard. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) is optional for adjacent host context; its documented `vmstat.sh` input and `vmstat` source type are not the primary event contract for this detector.

spl:
index=os sourcetype="linux:vmstat_swap" source=linux_vmstat_swap host=* earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m
| fields _time host collector_schema collector_status sample_epoch boot_id page_size_bytes pswpin_pages pswpout_pages pgmajfault_total
| eval collector_schema=tonumber(collector_schema), sample_epoch=tonumber(sample_epoch), page_size_bytes=tonumber(page_size_bytes), pswpin_pages=tonumber(pswpin_pages), pswpout_pages=tonumber(pswpout_pages), pgmajfault_total=tonumber(pgmajfault_total)
| where collector_schema=1 AND collector_status="ok" AND isnotnull(host) AND isnotnull(sample_epoch) AND isnotnull(boot_id) AND page_size_bytes>=1024 AND pswpin_pages>=0 AND pswpout_pages>=0 AND pgmajfault_total>=0
| stats max(pswpin_pages) as pswpin_pages max(pswpout_pages) as pswpout_pages max(pgmajfault_total) as pgmajfault_total max(page_size_bytes) as page_size_bytes by host boot_id sample_epoch
| sort 0 host boot_id sample_epoch
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(sample_epoch) as previous_sample_epoch last(page_size_bytes) as previous_page_size_bytes last(pswpin_pages) as previous_pswpin_pages last(pswpout_pages) as previous_pswpout_pages last(pgmajfault_total) as previous_pgmajfault_total by host boot_id
| eval elapsed_seconds=sample_epoch-previous_sample_epoch
| eval pswpin_delta_pages=if(pswpin_pages>=previous_pswpin_pages,pswpin_pages-previous_pswpin_pages,null()), pswpout_delta_pages=if(pswpout_pages>=previous_pswpout_pages,pswpout_pages-previous_pswpout_pages,null()), pgmajfault_delta=if(pgmajfault_total>=previous_pgmajfault_total,pgmajfault_total-previous_pgmajfault_total,null())
| eval swapin_kib_s=if(elapsed_seconds>0 AND elapsed_seconds<=150 AND page_size_bytes=previous_page_size_bytes,pswpin_delta_pages*page_size_bytes/1024/elapsed_seconds,null()), swapout_kib_s=if(elapsed_seconds>0 AND elapsed_seconds<=150 AND page_size_bytes=previous_page_size_bytes,pswpout_delta_pages*page_size_bytes/1024/elapsed_seconds,null()), major_faults_per_second=if(elapsed_seconds>0 AND elapsed_seconds<=150,pgmajfault_delta/elapsed_seconds,null())
| where isnotnull(swapin_kib_s)
| eval _time=sample_epoch
| bin _time span=1m
| stats avg(swapin_kib_s) as swapin_kib_s avg(swapout_kib_s) as swapout_kib_s max(major_faults_per_second) as major_faults_per_second latest(page_size_bytes) as page_size_bytes count as rate_samples by host boot_id _time
| eval candidate_start=relative_time(now(),"-10m@m"), candidate_end=relative_time(now(),"-5m@m"), swapin_threshold_kib_s=1024
| where _time>=candidate_start AND _time<candidate_end
| eval swapin_breach=if(swapin_kib_s>=swapin_threshold_kib_s,1,0)
| stats count as observed_buckets sum(swapin_breach) as breach_buckets min(_time) as window_start max(_time) as window_end avg(swapin_kib_s) as average_swapin_kib_s max(swapin_kib_s) as maximum_swapin_kib_s avg(swapout_kib_s) as average_swapout_kib_s max(major_faults_per_second) as maximum_major_faults_per_second min(rate_samples) as minimum_rate_samples latest(page_size_bytes) as page_size_bytes latest(swapin_threshold_kib_s) as swapin_threshold_kib_s by host boot_id
| where observed_buckets=5 AND breach_buckets>=3
| eval window_end=window_end+60, average_swapin_kib_s=round(average_swapin_kib_s,1), maximum_swapin_kib_s=round(maximum_swapin_kib_s,1), average_swapout_kib_s=round(average_swapout_kib_s,1), maximum_major_faults_per_second=round(maximum_major_faults_per_second,2), severity="medium"
| sort 0 -maximum_swapin_kib_s host
| table host severity window_start window_end observed_buckets breach_buckets average_swapin_kib_s maximum_swapin_kib_s average_swapout_kib_s maximum_major_faults_per_second swapin_threshold_kib_s page_size_bytes minimum_rate_samples boot_id
description: Reports a Linux host when at least three of five complete, closed one-minute buckets average 1,024 KiB/s or more of swap-in traffic. It derives the rate from adjacent cumulative `pswpin` page counters, multiplies by the measured base page size, divides by observed elapsed time, separates boots, and rejects counter decreases, page-size changes, malformed samples, and collection gaps longer than 150 seconds.
value: Repeatedly reading evicted memory back from swap can add storage latency to application work and indicate that a host's active working set no longer fits comfortably in available memory. A unit-safe, complete-window signal gives platform teams an earlier triage point than swap occupancy alone while retaining swap-out and major-fault context and avoiding the stronger claim that one directional rate proves thrashing.
implementation: Deploy `TA-linux-vmstat-swap` to in-scope Linux Universal Forwarders and collect `/proc/vmstat`, host page size, boot ID, and sample epoch once per minute. Schedule `linux_vmstat_swap_in_rate_5m` every five minutes against delayed closed buckets. Start with a reviewed policy of at least 1,024 KiB/s in three of five minutes, then baseline by host and workload class; this threshold is a catalogue default, not a Linux, procps-ng, or Splunk recommendation.
scriptExample:
#!/bin/sh
set -u

SCHEMA=1
VMSTAT_FILE=/proc/vmstat
BOOT_ID_FILE=/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
sample_epoch=$(date +%s 2>/dev/null) || exit 1

emit_error() {
  printf 'collector_schema=%s collector_status=read_error sample_epoch=%s error_code=%s\n' "$SCHEMA" "$sample_epoch" "$1"
  exit 0
}

[ -r "$VMSTAT_FILE" ] || emit_error vmstat_unreadable
[ -r "$BOOT_ID_FILE" ] || emit_error boot_id_unreadable
page_size_bytes=$(getconf PAGE_SIZE 2>/dev/null) || emit_error page_size_unavailable
boot_id=$(tr -d '\n' < "$BOOT_ID_FILE" 2>/dev/null) || emit_error boot_id_read_failed
counters=$(awk '
  $1 == "pswpin" { pin=$2 }
  $1 == "pswpout" { pout=$2 }
  $1 == "pgmajfault" { maj=$2 }
  END {
    if (pin == "" || pout == "" || maj == "") exit 1
    printf "%s %s %s", pin, pout, maj
  }
' "$VMSTAT_FILE") || emit_error vmstat_fields_missing
set -- $counters
[ "$#" -eq 3 ] || emit_error vmstat_fields_invalid
for value in "$page_size_bytes" "$1" "$2" "$3"; do
  case "$value" in ''|*[!0-9]*) emit_error nonnumeric_counter ;; esac
done
[ -n "$boot_id" ] || emit_error boot_id_empty
printf 'collector_schema=%s collector_status=ok sample_epoch=%s boot_id=%s page_size_bytes=%s pswpin_pages=%s pswpout_pages=%s pgmajfault_total=%s\n' "$SCHEMA" "$sample_epoch" "$boot_id" "$page_size_bytes" "$1" "$2" "$3"
visualization: Plot derived `swapin_kib_s` and `swapout_kib_s` on a per-host KiB/s timechart with a clearly labelled 1,024 KiB/s policy line; place `major_faults_per_second` on a separate axis or panel. Add a latest-first findings table with the evidence fields and a collection-health panel for missing minutes, non-`ok` status, counter decreases, duplicate samples, and stale hosts. Provide drilldowns to memory availability, swap occupancy, PSI, per-process or cgroup memory, storage latency, OOM events, and recent changes. Never graph raw `pswpin_pages`, `pswpout_pages`, or `pgmajfault_total` as rates or mix pages, kB, KB, KiB, and percentages on one axis.
dataModelAcceleration: No CIM-accelerated equivalent is asserted. Keep the primary detector on the local raw-event contract; CIM panels may provide context only.

knownFalsePositives:
Every result represents a real derived swap-in rate under this event contract, but the activity may be expected or may not imply user-visible impact.

1. **Application or host warm-up** — A service restart, reboot recovery, failover, or scheduled worker activation can fault previously swapped anonymous pages back into memory. Verify boot and service start times, readiness duration, latency, and whether the rate falls after warm-up. The boot guard prevents a cross-reboot delta but does not make post-boot swap-in abnormal by definition.

2. **Approved memory-pressure or resilience test** — `stress-ng`, chaos exercises, failover drills, and swap-device tests can intentionally generate rates above policy. Require the exact host, bounded UTC interval, owner, test plan, and change record; retain the unsuppressed finding as control evidence while suppressing notification delivery only.

3. **Batch, analytics, backup, or restore phase change** — A large job can revisit memory that was legitimately evicted during another phase. Correlate job identity, normal phase timing, throughput, swap-out, major faults, PSI, and application SLOs. Use a separate host-class policy instead of exempting all batch systems.

4. **Virtual-machine ballooning or host overcommit operation** — Hypervisor reclamation can force guest pages out and later create real guest swap-in when memory is returned or touched again. Confirm balloon metrics, reservation changes, migration activity, and the hypervisor incident before assigning the condition solely to the guest workload.

5. **Hibernate or suspend resume** — A system restoring memory state from swap can produce substantial swap-in. This is uncommon for production servers but normal for fleets that deliberately suspend. Scope such hosts by documented role and correlate systemd sleep/resume records; do not create an undocumented global exception.

6. **Threshold mismatch across host classes** — 1 MiB/s can be serious on a small latency-sensitive node and harmless during a short phase on a large host with fast storage. Baseline web, database, virtual-desktop, batch, and development classes separately. Preserve unit conversion, complete-window checks, and source-health monitoring when changing the threshold or required breach count.

7. **Duplicate collectors, host collision, or delayed events** — Two scripted stanzas, cloned host names, forwarding backlog, or incorrect clocks can distort adjacent samples. The SPL groups by boot ID, uses collector epoch, collapses exact timestamps, and rejects long gaps, but operators must still compare source, forwarder identity, `_indextime`, event counts, and raw counters before escalation.

**Safe suppression:** keep the catalogue SPL unchanged and apply any deployment exception after the final finding. Key the lookup on exact `host` with `valid_from_epoch`, `valid_until_epoch`, `owner`, `reason`, `ticket`, and approver; reject wildcards and non-expiring rows. Preserve suppressed matches in a review panel. Never suppress source errors, stale collectors, counter resets, all hosts in an environment, or raw events before `streamstats`, because pre-delta filtering can splice unrelated counter observations.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and measurement contract

Assign a Linux platform owner, a Splunk content owner, and a workload escalation path before deployment. Run a supported Universal Forwarder in the same host and procfs namespace that the use case is meant to describe. The forwarder service identity needs execute permission on the packaged shell script and read access to `/proc/vmstat`, `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, and the system page-size interface exposed through `getconf PAGE_SIZE`. These interfaces are normally readable without privilege, but hardened procfs mounts, containers, and service sandboxes can change visibility. Test as the actual forwarder account. Do not grant unrestricted `sudo`, add write permission to procfs, alter swap, or change `vm.swappiness` for collection.

Treat the unit and lifetime contract as part of the detector, not as display trivia. Linux `/proc/vmstat` exposes `pswpin` as a cumulative count of pages swapped in. It is not a current rate and it is not expressed in kB, KB, KiB, or bytes. The base page size is host-specific; 4,096 bytes is common but must not be hard-coded. The collector therefore records `page_size_bytes`, and the search computes `(current_pswpin - previous_pswpin) * page_size_bytes / 1024 / elapsed_seconds`. The result is KiB/s. A raw difference of 15,360 pages over 60 seconds is 1,024 KiB/s only when the measured page size is 4,096 bytes.

The procps-ng `vmstat(8)` utility labels `si` as memory swapped in from disk per second. Its implementation reads the kernel swap-in counter, applies page-size conversion, and derives a rate. The first report is special: the manual says it reports averages since the last reboot, while subsequent reports describe the requested sampling interval. Never ingest one un-delayed `vmstat` line and call its `si` value a current one-minute rate. For a point-in-time comparison, use a delayed sample such as `vmstat -y -S K 60 2` where the installed procps-ng supports `-y`; compare the second report and confirm the selected unit. The catalogue search independently derives the rate from counters so it can enforce counter lifetime, elapsed-time, completeness, and reset rules.

Do not assume `sourcetype=vmstat` from `Splunk_TA_nix` contains an extracted field named `si`. Current Splunk documentation maps that source type to `vmstat.sh`, but the documented source-type table does not promise this native periodic-column field. Historical Linux implementations of the add-on script use summary-style output and fields such as cumulative page or swap-out values. Modifying a vendor script in place would be overwritten by upgrades and would blur the event contract. This use case instead uses a small deployment-owned app and a distinct source type. The optional add-on remains useful for memory percentage, process, CPU, and inventory context.

`pswpout` and `pgmajfault` are collected only as investigation context. `pswpout` is another cumulative page counter and receives the same conversion to KiB/s. `pgmajfault` is a cumulative major-fault count and is divided only by elapsed seconds because it counts events, not pages or bytes. Neither field participates in the alert gate. A high swap-in rate alone does not prove thrashing: pages may be read back without simultaneous swap-out or measurable stall. UC-1.1.100 intentionally provides an earlier, lower-confidence directional signal; a separate thrashing detector should require bidirectional activity and impact evidence.

## Step 1 — Package and configure one-minute collection

Create a locally managed app named `TA-linux-vmstat-swap`. Place the `scriptExample` at `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA-linux-vmstat-swap/bin/collect_vmstat_swap.sh`, make it executable, and make its code writable only by the deployment administrator. Do not place it in `Splunk_TA_nix/bin` or edit that add-on's defaults. The script invokes only `date`, `getconf`, `tr`, and `awk`; verify their resolved paths and behavior in any restricted forwarder service environment. It emits one line of key-value data. Mandatory read failures emit `collector_status=read_error` with a bounded error code instead of publishing zeros.

Configure `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA-linux-vmstat-swap/local/inputs.conf`:

```ini
[script://./bin/collect_vmstat_swap.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = * * * * *
index = os
source = linux_vmstat_swap
sourcetype = linux:vmstat_swap
```

The cron expression requests one launch on each minute boundary. Splunk scripted-input documentation states that only one invocation is kept per instance; the collector must therefore finish in well under one minute. A numeric `interval=60` is also legal, but numeric intervals are measured from script completion and can drift across minute boundaries. If local policy prohibits cron-form scripted intervals, retain the numeric interval and validate actual bucket completeness before using the five-bucket alert. `index=os` is a deployment convention, not a Splunk requirement; substitute the approved event index consistently in the input, role, dashboard, controls, and SPL.

One healthy host produces approximately 1,440 short events per day. Measure serialized event size and actual license usage on canaries instead of treating this count as a byte estimate. For Splunk Cloud Platform, run the script on a customer-managed Universal Forwarder and forward the result; do not imply that a shell collector runs on the managed search tier.

Configure line handling and search-time extraction in the app deployed to the appropriate parsing and search tiers:

```ini
[linux:vmstat_swap]
SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false
LINE_BREAKER = ([\r\n]+)
TRUNCATE = 0
DATETIME_CONFIG = CURRENT
KV_MODE = auto
```

`DATETIME_CONFIG=CURRENT` timestamps ingestion close to collection, but the detector uses the explicit numeric `sample_epoch` for rate intervals and bucket assignment. `KV_MODE=auto` extracts the `key=value` pairs at search time. Do not add a second indexed extraction for the same fields. Keep `collector_status=read_error` events and alert on their presence separately; a failed read is unknown telemetry, not zero swap-in.

Run the script manually as the forwarder identity. Require `collector_schema=1`, `collector_status=ok`, a nonempty UUID-like boot ID, positive numeric page size, and nonnegative numeric counters. Compare the event with `getconf PAGE_SIZE`, `cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, and `awk '$1=="pswpin" || $1=="pswpout" || $1=="pgmajfault" {print}' /proc/vmstat`. Then verify the winning stanza with `splunk btool inputs list --debug` and search `index=os sourcetype=linux:vmstat_swap source=linux_vmstat_swap earliest=-10m | table _time _indextime host collector_status sample_epoch boot_id page_size_bytes pswpin_pages pswpout_pages pgmajfault_total`. Expect one healthy event per minute per host and increasing sample epochs.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the saved search

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_vmstat_swap_in_rate_5m`. Schedule it every five minutes on minute boundaries with cron `*/5 * * * *`, trigger when result count is greater than zero, and preserve `earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m`. The search reads enough history to obtain a predecessor but evaluates only five closed candidate minutes from ten through five minutes before dispatch. The five-minute indexing delay reduces partial buckets and late-arrival churn. Measure `_indextime-sample_epoch` in the real deployment and lengthen the delay if necessary; do not evaluate the newest open minute merely to reduce alert latency.

### Understanding the SPL

The first `eval` converts the event fields to numbers. The `where` clause accepts only schema version 1, healthy collector status, required identities, a plausible positive page size, and nonnegative counters. The first `stats` collapses exact duplicate host, boot, and collector-epoch rows using maxima rather than summing cumulative values. Investigate duplicates separately; this collapse prevents one duplicate from creating multiple adjacent-rate rows but cannot make a host-name collision safe.

`sort 0 host boot_id sample_epoch` is mandatory because `streamstats` consumes rows in order. `streamstats current=f window=1` carries the immediately preceding sample within the same host and boot ID. A reboot begins a new series and cannot be compared with the previous boot. The delta expressions require nondecreasing counters. A counter decrease is treated as a reset or malformed observation and becomes null, not a negative rate. The next valid adjacent pair can resume, but the final five-bucket completeness rule prevents an interval reset inside the candidate window from quietly satisfying the alert.

`elapsed_seconds` comes from collector epochs rather than assuming exactly 60 seconds. Positive intervals up to 150 seconds are eligible; longer gaps are discarded so an hour of cumulative swap-in cannot be divided down and presented as current activity. The current and previous page sizes must match. The page delta is multiplied by bytes per page, divided by 1,024 to produce KiB, and divided by elapsed seconds. This deliberately says KiB/s, not ambiguous `KB/s`. Swap-out uses the same calculation. Major faults are count events, so their delta is divided by seconds without page-size conversion.

The one-minute `bin` normalizes small launch jitter. If more than one eligible pair lands in a bucket, `stats` averages the rates and records `rate_samples`; a collection-health panel should expose values other than one. The candidate filter selects exactly five closed minute buckets. `swapin_breach` is one when that bucket's average is at least 1,024 KiB/s. The final aggregation requires all five buckets to exist and at least three to breach. Thus three isolated breached minutes within the five-minute window qualify; this is repeated elevated activity, not a claim of three consecutive minutes. If policy requires consecutiveness, implement and test a separate run-length rule rather than changing the narrative while leaving this SPL unchanged.

The 1,024 KiB/s floor and three-of-five persistence rule are transparent initial catalogue policy, not defaults recommended by the kernel, procps-ng, or Splunk. One MiB/s has very different impact on a small latency-sensitive VM and a large batch server with fast swap. Baseline by host class using percentiles, application latency, PSI, storage latency, swap occupancy, and known workload phases. Keep the resolved threshold in every result. Do not tune by changing the units, dropping completeness checks, or averaging all hosts together.

The output severity is medium because this directional rate is an investigation signal rather than proof of service impact. Route per host and boot ID, throttle repeated notifications for at least the evaluated five-minute window, and retain every scheduled result for trend review. Do not have the alert automatically kill a process, drop caches, disable swap, change swappiness, resize a VM, or restart a workload.

There is no faithful CIM `tstats` replacement. A memory-used percentage and a swap-used percentage are gauges; they cannot reconstruct adjacent `pswpin` counter deltas, base page size, boot boundaries, collection gaps, or the exact directional rate. Use CIM-normalized memory panels as context only.

## Step 3 — Validate arithmetic, controls, and source completeness

First validate one real adjacent pair by hand. Record two raw events and compute `(new_pswpin_pages-old_pswpin_pages) * page_size_bytes / 1024 / (new_sample_epoch-old_sample_epoch)`. Compare the result with the search's `swapin_kib_s` before final aggregation. Repeat for swap-out. Compute `(new_pgmajfault_total-old_pgmajfault_total)/elapsed_seconds` and compare the fault context. If any arithmetic differs, inspect extraction, numeric conversion, ordering, event duplication, page size, and timestamp selection before tuning policy.

Compare a controlled interval with procps-ng. Run `vmstat -y -S K 60 2` where supported and use the second report, because the first is since-boot average. The command's interval and the collector's adjacent interval will not necessarily start at the same instant, so expect close directional agreement during steady activity rather than byte-for-byte identity during bursts. Confirm the installed manual's unit behavior; `-S K` selects 1,024-byte units for `si` in current procps-ng. Never compare the raw `pswpin` page total directly to `si`, and never label `vmstat -s` cumulative `pages swapped in` as a rate.

Execute the positive control with fixed absolute epochs. At a 4,096-byte page size, each 30,720-page increase over 60 seconds is `30720*4096/1024/60 = 2048` KiB/s. Three such intervals plus two zero intervals produce five observed buckets and three breaches. Inspect the pre-aggregation rows, then require the final maximum of 2,048 KiB/s and medium severity. Keep swap-out and major-fault counters nondecreasing so context rates are valid but do not affect the gate.

Execute the negative control with only two breached intervals. It must produce no finding despite a maximum rate of 2,048 KiB/s. Then run each guard independently: same-boot counter decrease, boot-ID change, page-size change, 151-second gap, missing candidate bucket, nonnumeric counter, exact duplicate event, and `read_error` status. A reset, identity change, unit change, long gap, malformed row, or unhealthy collector must not create a rate. Fewer than five candidate buckets must not alert. Exact duplicates must not be summed.

Validate source health independently over at least 24 hours: `index=os sourcetype=linux:vmstat_swap earliest=-24h | timechart span=1m count by host limit=0`. Also report latest sample age, non-`ok` statuses, page-size changes, multiple boot IDs, duplicate host/epoch rows, and `_indextime-sample_epoch` percentiles. Absence of a detector finding is not proof that collection is healthy. This editorial review did not execute the shell collector, ingest fixtures, run the SPL on Splunk, or compare a live `vmstat` interval, so keep `status=draft` until a qualified operator performs and signs those tests.

## Step 4 — Operationalize triage and evidence

Build the dashboard described in `visualization`. Keep rate and capacity gauges separate: `swapin_kib_s` describes movement per second, while swap-used percentage describes occupancy at an instant. Plot swap-in and swap-out together because their relationship matters, but do not call unidirectional activity thrashing. Add major-fault rate, memory PSI where available, `MemAvailable`, swap occupancy, storage latency, and workload SLOs as aligned panels. A result with high swap-in and low swap-out can be a warm-up; high values in both directions plus sustained full PSI is stronger evidence of harmful churn.

The response runbook should: (1) verify five complete source buckets, one boot ID, stable page size, expected sample gaps, and no duplicate collector; (2) inspect raw `pswpin` arithmetic and compare a delayed `vmstat` sample; (3) correlate `pswpout`, major faults, PSI, memory availability, swap occupancy, block-device latency, OOM or killed-process logs, and application latency; (4) check deployments, service starts, batch phases, backup or restore activity, VM ballooning, migration, and host overcommit; (5) identify process and cgroup consumers with approved tools such as `smem`, `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup`, cgroup `memory.current`, `memory.swap.current`, and `memory.pressure`; and (6) involve the workload owner before remediation.

System-wide `/proc/vmstat` cannot name the responsible process or cgroup. A process that touches pages can cause swap-in even when another process created the earlier pressure. Preserve this distinction in tickets. Do not infer that the process with the largest resident set caused every swap-in, and do not expose command lines or tenant identifiers broadly in dashboards.

Retain the artifacts listed in `evidence` under local operations policy. The base use case intentionally does not invent an `audit_evidence` index, universal retention period, SOC ownership, or weekly export. If the organization copies results to a controlled evidence store, document access, retention, search revision, threshold revision, and time synchronization. Those records demonstrate monitoring behavior only; they do not establish regulatory compliance or prove root cause.

Review the threshold after changes to RAM, swap device, kernel, page size, virtualization policy, workload class, or service SLO. Review collection after forwarder or app upgrades. Maintain separate policy rows by governed host class if needed, and fail closed when a required policy row is missing or expired. Never silently default missing thresholds to zero.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and suppress safely

- **No events:** run the collector as the forwarder service identity; verify app deployment, execute bit, procfs visibility, `getconf`, the effective stanza, route to the selected index, and search-role access. Inspect `splunkd.log` for the exact script path and stderr. A forwarder inside a container may see only that namespace's procfs.
- **`collector_status=read_error`:** use `error_code` to distinguish unreadable procfs, missing counters, page-size failure, and boot-ID failure. Do not coalesce absent counters to zero or mark the host healthy because another add-on source type is present.
- **Raw text but null fields:** verify `sourcetype=linux:vmstat_swap`, search-tier `props.conf`, app replication, and `KV_MODE=auto`. Check that another props stanza has not disabled extraction. Do not use `multikv`; this event is key-value, not a table.
- **Null derived rate:** the row may be the first sample for a boot, follow a counter decrease, have a nonpositive or greater-than-150-second gap, or have a changed page size. Inspect the two raw events selected by ordering. Null is an intentional guard, not zero activity.
- **Implausibly large rate:** verify page size is bytes, not KiB; check host-name collisions, duplicate deployment clients, stale clocks, merged environments, corrupted counters, and sample epoch. A 4,096-byte page must contribute four KiB, not 4,096 KiB.
- **Rate differs from `vmstat`:** ensure comparison uses the second delayed report, matching 1,024-byte units and overlapping time windows. Short bursts, integer display rounding, different interval boundaries, and command-version behavior can explain small differences. Reconcile raw counter deltas before changing SPL.
- **High swap-in with no result:** verify all five closed candidate buckets, three breaches, the delayed time window, indexing latency, and exact threshold. One spike or two breached minutes is intentionally below policy.
- **Persistent findings:** determine whether policy is mis-sized for the host class or whether workload working set, leak, overcommit, ballooning, or swap-device behavior changed. Fix capacity or workload policy through change control; a permanent alert exception is not remediation.

Apply only the bounded post-result suppression contract in `knownFalsePositives`. Preserve source-health alerts and unsuppressed findings. Never filter raw events before `streamstats`, because removing a maintenance interval can make the search compare counters across the excluded gap and misstate a rate. Re-run arithmetic, positive, negative, reset, gap, and completeness controls after any collector, extraction, SPL, threshold, kernel, or forwarder change.
grandmaExplanation: We watch when a Linux server repeatedly has to pull working memory back from its slower disk space. That warning helps the team investigate memory pressure before the extra waiting turns into a noticeable slowdown.
